questions.stem: A 58-year-old man is found to have an eGFR of 52 mL/min/1.73 m² on a routine physical. Repeat testing 4 months later shows an eGFR of 50 mL/min/1.73 m² with a urine albumin/creatinine ratio of 12 mg/g and a normal urinalysis. Which feature of his presentation most directly satisfies the diagnostic criteria for chronic kidney disease?
choices: Albuminuria above the standard diagnostic cutoff
Decreased eGFR persisting for at least 3 months
An abnormal urinalysis with cells or casts
Imaging evidence of bilateral polycystic kidneys
A pathologic biopsy showing glomerular disease
explanations: Incorrect. CKD requires an ACR >30 mg/g; this patient's ACR of 12 mg/g is below that threshold.
Correct. CKD is defined as decreased kidney function (eGFR <60 mL/min/1.73 m²) and/or kidney damage present for ≥3 months; his eGFR has been <60 for 4 months.
Incorrect. His urinalysis is normal, so urinary sediment abnormalities are not what establishes the diagnosis here.
Incorrect. No imaging abnormalities are described in this case.
Incorrect. No biopsy has been performed, so pathologic findings are not the basis of diagnosis.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes is told she has chronic kidney disease after her labs return with an eGFR of 48 mL/min/1.73 m² and a urine albumin/creatinine ratio of 220 mg/g, both confirmed on repeat testing. Using the categorization scheme described in the brick, how is her CKD classified?
explanations: Incorrect. G2 is eGFR 60-89 with ACR <30 mg/g; her values are lower and higher, respectively.
Correct. eGFR 45-59 is G3a, and ACR 30-300 mg/g is A2, giving CKD G3aA2.
Incorrect. G3b is eGFR 30-44 and A3 is ACR >300 mg/g; her numbers do not reach those categories.
Incorrect. G4 requires eGFR 15-29, which she does not have.
Incorrect. G5 requires eGFR <15 (kidney failure), which she does not have.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man with diabetes presents with fatigue, poor appetite, generalized weakness, itching, and intermittent nausea over the past month. His eGFR is 12 mL/min/1.73 m². Which mechanism described in the brick best explains his constellation of symptoms?
choices: Iron deficiency from poor intestinal absorption of dietary iron
Hypocalcemia from impaired renal calcitriol production
Inability to excrete waste products at low GFR
explanations: Incorrect. Iron deficiency contributes to anemia and fatigue but does not by itself produce itching, vomiting, or anorexia.
Incorrect. Hypocalcemia from low calcitriol contributes to bone disease, not directly to the uremic symptom complex described.
Correct. When eGFR drops below 10-15 mL/min/1.73 m², the body cannot excrete waste products, producing fatigue, anorexia, weakness, itching, and vomiting (uremic symptoms).
Incorrect. Hyperkalemia is typically asymptomatic until cardiac arrhythmias develop and would not cause itching or anorexia.
Incorrect. Volume overload causes edema and dyspnea rather than the uremic symptom cluster described.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man with a 12-year history of type 2 diabetes mellitus presents for follow-up. According to the brick, which of the following is the most common cause of chronic kidney disease in the United States and the leading reason for both dialysis and transplantation?
explanations: Incorrect. Hypertension worsens other kidney diseases, but the brick states it rarely causes ESRD on its own.
Correct. Diabetes mellitus is the most common cause of CKD in the US and the leading reason for both dialysis and transplantation.
Incorrect. ADPKD is the most important cystic cause of CKD but is not the overall most common cause.
Incorrect. Obstructive nephropathy is one cause of CKD but is not the leading driver of dialysis.
Incorrect. Modern NSAIDs only meaningfully cause CKD at very high doses or with concurrent insults; they are not the leading cause.

questions.stem: A 61-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes for 8 years has a serum creatinine that has been rising over the past 2 years; her eGFR is now 42 mL/min/1.73 m². Repeated urine albumin/creatinine ratios are <30 mg/g. Which of the following best explains her presentation?
choices: Absent diabetic kidney disease since albuminuria is lacking
Non-proteinuric diabetic kidney disease in type 2
Acute tubular necrosis from IV contrast
Hypertensive nephrosclerosis with hyaline arteriolar disease
Obstructive nephropathy from a ureteral stone
explanations: Incorrect. The brick specifically notes that diabetic patients can present with elevated creatinine without proteinuria.
Correct. Non-proteinuric diabetic kidney disease occurs in approximately 40% of patients with type 2 diabetes and 20% of those with type 1 diabetes.
Incorrect. ATN is acute, not a 2-year progressive decline in GFR, and no contrast exposure is described.
Incorrect. While possible, the brick frames her clinical picture as classic non-proteinuric diabetic kidney disease.
Incorrect. No obstruction or stone history is described.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old hypertensive man undergoes a kidney biopsy that shows thickening of small arteries and arterioles with eosinophilic deposits of plasma proteins (including inactive C3b) within the damaged arteriolar walls. Which process is depicted?
explanations: Correct. In hypertensive nephrosclerosis, hypertension causes plasma proteins (eg, inactive C3b) to leak through the endothelium and deposit in arteriolar walls, producing hyaline arteriosclerosis.
Incorrect. FSGS is a glomerular lesion, not an arteriolar wall deposit of plasma proteins.
Incorrect. ATN is an acute tubular injury without arteriolar wall deposits.
Incorrect. PAN is a vasculitis of medium-sized vessels, not the small arteriolar hyaline deposition described.
Incorrect. Tubulointerstitial fibrosis affects the interstitium, not arteriolar walls.

questions.stem: A 47-year-old man with longstanding renal artery stenosis has progressive CKD attributed to renovascular disease. According to the brick, which of the following is also categorized as a small-vessel vascular cause of CKD?
explanations: Incorrect. Renal artery stenosis is the large-vessel example given in the brick, not a small-vessel cause.
Correct. The brick lists chronic hypertension, microangiopathy, and vasculitis due to polyarteritis nodosa as small-vessel causes of renovascular CKD.
Incorrect. ADPKD is a cystic, hereditary cause of CKD, not a small-vessel disease.
Incorrect. ATN is a tubulointerstitial cause, not a vascular one.
Incorrect. BPH causes obstructive nephropathy, a tubulointerstitial cause.

questions.stem: A 78-year-old man with longstanding benign prostatic hyperplasia and recurrent kidney stones presents with an eGFR of 38 mL/min/1.73 m². Imaging shows bilateral hydronephrosis. Through what mechanism described in the brick does this lead to chronic kidney disease?
choices: Direct glomerular capillary tuft injury from immune-mediated mechanisms
Pressure from urine buildup damages tubules and interstitium
Cystic replacement of the renal parenchyma by enlarging fluid-filled cysts
Hyaline arteriosclerosis of small renal arterioles from chronic hypertension
Immune-complex deposition in the glomerular basement membrane
explanations: Incorrect. Glomerular tuft injury is the mechanism in glomerular diseases like diabetic or lupus nephropathy.

Correct. Obstructive nephropathy occurs when chronic obstruction (eg, BPH, longstanding stones) raises pressure in the kidney, damaging tubules and interstitium and producing interstitial fibrosis with declining GFR.
Incorrect. Cystic replacement describes ADPKD, not obstruction.
Incorrect. Hyaline arteriosclerosis is the lesion of hypertensive nephrosclerosis.
Incorrect. Immune-complex deposition is a glomerulonephritis mechanism, not the obstructive mechanism described.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old woman with stage 3 CKD takes ibuprofen daily for arthritis. According to the brick, modern NSAIDs most often cause a reduction in GFR under which circumstance?
choices: When used at standard doses in patients with completely normal kidneys
When combined with another insult such as volume depletion or diuretic use
Only when used continuously for less than 2 weeks at standard outpatient doses
Only after intravenous administration in a hospitalized patient
Only when combined with SGLT2 inhibitors at high therapeutic doses
explanations: Incorrect. The brick specifies that current NSAIDs are usually associated with CKD only at very high doses or in combination with other insults.
Correct. NSAIDs typically reduce GFR when combined with another insult such as volume depletion, low blood pressure, or concurrent diuretic or ACE/ARB use.
Incorrect. Duration is not the qualifier given in the brick; concurrent insults are.
Incorrect. NSAIDs are oral or topical in this context; the brick does not invoke an IV route.
Incorrect. SGLT2 inhibitors are not mentioned as the relevant interaction; diuretics and ACE/ARBs are.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old man with a family history of kidney failure undergoes CT imaging that shows both kidneys massively enlarged with parenchyma replaced by numerous fluid-filled cysts. According to the brick, what is the most important cystic disease that causes CKD?
choices: Simple renal cysts found incidentally on imaging
Medullary sponge kidney with collecting duct ectasia
Acquired cystic kidney disease in long-term dialysis
Alport syndrome with hereditary glomerular involvement
explanations: Incorrect. Simple cysts do not progressively distort the kidney and rarely cause CKD.
Incorrect. Medullary sponge kidney is not the cystic disease highlighted by the brick.
Correct. The brick states that the most important cystic disease causing CKD is autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD), in which cysts distort the kidney structure and reduce GFR.
Incorrect. Acquired cystic disease is a complication of dialysis, not the principal cystic cause of CKD discussed.
Incorrect. Alport syndrome is a hereditary glomerular disease, not a cystic disease.

questions.stem: An 18-year-old man presents with hematuria and proteinuria. He also reports progressive sensorineural hearing loss and has anterior lenticonus on eye exam. Which hereditary cause of CKD described in the brick best fits?
explanations: Incorrect. ADPKD presents with cysts and hypertension, not eye and ear disease.

Correct. The brick describes Alport syndrome as a hereditary cause of CKD that initially presents with small amounts of hematuria and proteinuria, progresses to ESKD, and often has accompanying eye or ear disease.
Incorrect. Diabetic kidney disease is acquired and tied to longstanding diabetes, not to eye/ear hereditary findings.
Incorrect. Hypertensive nephrosclerosis is acquired and is not associated with sensorineural hearing loss.
Incorrect. PAN is a vasculitis without the hereditary, eye/ear-disease pattern described.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old woman is being worked up for newly discovered CKD. Per the brick, which test is used specifically to assess the degree of albuminuria as part of the diagnostic evaluation?
explanations: Incorrect. Serum creatinine is used to calculate eGFR, not to quantify albuminuria.
Correct. The albumin/creatinine ratio (ACR) is the test the brick lists for assessing the degree of albuminuria.
Incorrect. Ultrasound assesses for echogenic kidneys, ADPKD, other cysts, and stones, but not albuminuria.
Incorrect. Biopsy assesses for autoimmune glomerular disease or unknown-cause CKD, not for albuminuria quantification.
Incorrect. Cystatin C is not the test highlighted in this brick for albuminuria.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man with CKD has heavy proteinuria and his urinalysis shows acanthocytes. According to the brick, what is the most appropriate next diagnostic step to clarify the underlying cause?
explanations: Incorrect. Repeating creatinine does not address the suspicion of an autoimmune glomerular process.
Correct. Kidney biopsy is obtained when there is concern for autoimmune glomerular disease based on heavy proteinuria or sediment findings such as acanthocytes that suggest glomerulonephritis.
Incorrect. Renal artery Doppler evaluates renal artery stenosis, not glomerulonephritis.
Incorrect. A 24-hour sodium does not diagnose glomerular disease.
Incorrect. Plain films are not part of the CKD workup described in the brick.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old patient undergoes renal ultrasound during CKD evaluation. According to the brick, what is the kidney ultrasound primarily used to assess?
choices: Glomerular filtration rate calculated from creatinine
Echogenic kidneys, cysts, and kidney stones
Tubular acidification capacity by ammonium chloride loading
explanations: Incorrect. eGFR is calculated from serum creatinine, not from ultrasound.
Correct. Per the brick, kidney ultrasound is used to assess for echogenic kidneys, autosomal dominant kidney disease, other cysts, and kidney stones.
Incorrect. Albuminuria is quantified with the ACR, not ultrasound.
Incorrect. Tubular acidification is not assessed by ultrasound.
Incorrect. EPO is measured in blood, not by imaging.

questions.stem: A 59-year-old woman with diabetes and CKD G3aA2 is being counseled on lifestyle changes that prevent decline of kidney function. Which of the following is the daily sodium target the brick recommends?
explanations: Incorrect. This is more restrictive than the brick's recommendation.
Incorrect. The brick recommends <2000 mg/day, not <1000.
Correct. The brick recommends sodium restriction of <2000 mg/day to lower blood pressure and reduce proteinuria.
Incorrect. This is too liberal; the brick's threshold is 2000 mg/day.
Incorrect. This is far above the brick's recommended limit.

questions.stem: A 56-year-old man with type 2 diabetes and CKD G3bA3 is referred for medical optimization. The brick recommends a HbA1c target of which of the following to help reduce CKD progression?
explanations: Incorrect. Below the brick's recommended threshold and not its stated target.
Incorrect. The brick gives 7%, not 6%, as the glycemic target for reducing CKD progression.
Correct. Glucose management to a HbA1c <7% in diabetes helps reduce CKD progression, per the brick.
Incorrect. Above the recommended threshold.
Incorrect. Far above the recommended threshold.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man with diabetic kidney disease and an ACR of 600 mg/g is started on a medication that lowers blood pressure, reduces proteinuria, and slows CKD progression. Which class of medication did he most likely receive?
explanations: Correct. ACE inhibitors or ARBs lower blood pressure, reduce proteinuria, and reduce CKD progression, per the brick.
Incorrect. Loop diuretics treat volume overload but the brick does not list them as agents that reduce proteinuria and slow CKD progression.
Incorrect. Thiazides are not the class identified in the brick for reducing proteinuria and slowing CKD progression.
Incorrect. Beta-blockers are not listed as proteinuria-reducing or CKD-slowing agents in the brick.
Incorrect. Calcium channel blockers are not the brick's specified class for these three effects.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes and CKD is started on a medication that, according to the brick, reduces CKD progression and reduces cardiovascular events. Which class is most consistent with this profile?
explanations: Correct. SGLT2 inhibitors reduce CKD progression and reduce cardiovascular events, per the brick.
Incorrect. Sulfonylureas are not described as having these renal/CV protective effects in the brick.
Incorrect. Thiazolidinediones are not mentioned as CKD-protective in the brick.
Incorrect. Alpha-glucosidase inhibitors are not part of the brick's CKD management plan.
Incorrect. Biguanides (metformin) are not the class described as reducing CKD progression and CV events.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old woman with CKD develops worsening hyperphosphatemia, then hypocalcemia and rising PTH. Per the brick, which of the following events initiates the cascade leading to renal osteodystrophy?
choices: Increased calcitriol synthesis by the kidney
Suppression of PTH by uremic toxins
explanations: Incorrect. Calcitriol synthesis is reduced (not increased) in CKD because FGF-23 inhibits 1-α hydroxylase.
Correct. Phosphate is retained in CKD due to decreased renal excretion, triggering ↑FGF-23, ↓calcitriol, hypocalcemia, and ↑PTH, ultimately producing renal osteodystrophy.
Incorrect. FGF-23 is increased, not decreased, in response to high serum phosphate.
Incorrect. PTH rises in this cascade; it is not suppressed.
Incorrect. Calcium absorption falls because low calcitriol reduces intestinal calcium uptake; hypocalcemia is the result.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man with stage 4 CKD has hemoglobin 9.2 g/dL with normal iron studies. Which mechanism described in the brick best explains his anemia at this stage?
choices: Decreased iron absorption in the duodenum and proximal small intestine
Hemolysis from circulating uremic toxins and oxidative stress
Bone marrow infiltration by light-chain amyloid deposits
explanations: Incorrect. Decreased iron absorption is more characteristic of early/moderate CKD (stages 1-3), and his iron studies are normal.
Correct. In advanced CKD (stages 4-5), the peritubular fibroblasts of the kidneys produce less erythropoietin, reducing red cell production.
Incorrect. The brick attributes shortened RBC survival to inflammation, but the dominant advanced-CKD mechanism it describes is reduced EPO.
Incorrect. Amyloid infiltration is not the mechanism described in the brick.
Incorrect. Splenic sequestration is not a CKD anemia mechanism described in the brick.

questions.stem: A 67-year-old man with CKD stage 4 and hemoglobin 8.5 g/dL is started on recombinant erythropoietin. According to the brick, which of the following is a known complication of EPO therapy?
explanations: Incorrect. Pancreatitis is not listed in the brick as an EPO complication.
Correct. Hypertension and venous thromboembolism are explicitly listed as complications of EPO therapy in the brick.
Incorrect. EPO does not cause hypoglycemia.
Incorrect. Pulmonary fibrosis is not an EPO complication described in the brick.
Incorrect. EPO is not associated with hypocalcemia in the brick.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man with CKD G4 and a history of myocardial infarction is being optimized medically. According to the brick, what is the most common cause of death in patients with CKD?
choices: Sepsis from a dialysis catheter access bloodstream infection
Hyperkalemic arrhythmia leading to sudden cardiac arrest
explanations: Incorrect. Sepsis is a risk in dialysis patients, but is not the most common cause of death described in the brick.
Correct. CKD is a coronary disease equivalent and accelerates atherosclerosis; cardiovascular death (eg, MI) is the most common cause of death in patients with CKD.
Incorrect. Hyperkalemia is a complication, but cardiovascular disease, not arrhythmia per se, is the brick's stated leading cause of death.
Incorrect. Uremic encephalopathy is uncommon and not the leading cause of death.
Incorrect. Bleeding from platelet dysfunction occurs but is not the leading cause of death.

questions.stem: A 71-year-old woman with CKD G4 has worsening LDL and total cholesterol. The brick recommends managing hyperlipidemia in CKD with which of the following to reduce cardiovascular mortality?
choices: Calorie restriction and bile acid sequestrant
explanations: Incorrect. The brick recommends a low-fat diet, not a high-fat diet, and does not specify fibrates.
Correct. Hyperlipidemia in CKD should be controlled with a low-fat diet and statin drugs, which decrease the elevated cardiovascular mortality risk in CKD.
Incorrect. The brick names statins, not niacin, for hyperlipidemia management.
Incorrect. Bile acid sequestrants are not the agents the brick recommends.
Incorrect. Diet alone is not the brick's recommendation; statins are explicitly included.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old woman with new CKD has an eGFR of 42 mL/min/1.73 m² and an ACR of 350 mg/g, with the cause not yet established. According to the brick, which of the following is an indication for referral to a nephrologist?
choices: Any patient with a diagnosis of diabetes mellitus, regardless of kidney function
Any patient with essential hypertension under treatment by a primary care physician
eGFR <60, especially with unknown cause or ACR >300 mg/g
Only after the patient develops overt uremic symptoms such as nausea or pruritus
Only when the eGFR falls below 10 mL/min/1.73 m² on repeat testing
explanations: Incorrect. Diabetes alone is not the referral threshold given in the brick.
Incorrect. Hypertension alone is not the referral threshold given in the brick.

Correct. The brick states referral should be considered when eGFR is <60 mL/min/1.73 m², especially if the cause is unknown, the eGFR is falling rapidly, or there are other risk factors such as ACR >300 mg/g.
Incorrect. Waiting for uremic symptoms delays appropriate care; referral is recommended much earlier.
Incorrect. Preparation for dialysis or transplant is at eGFR <20, and general referral is at <60 — not <10.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old man with CKD has had progressively declining kidney function over the past 2 years. His most recent eGFR is 18 mL/min/1.73 m². According to the brick, what is the appropriate next step at this eGFR?
choices: Start emergent dialysis immediately regardless of clinical symptoms or volume status
Begin preparations for dialysis or kidney transplantation
Stop all antihypertensive and renoprotective medications
Repeat labs in 1 year without further intervention
Permanently discontinue ACE inhibitor and SGLT2 inhibitor therapy
explanations: Incorrect. The brick says preparations begin at this eGFR; emergent initiation is reserved for indications like volume overload, resistant hyperkalemia, pericarditis, pleuritis, sensory problems, or confusion.
Correct. Preparations for dialysis or referral for kidney transplantation take place when the eGFR is <20 mL/min/1.73 m².
Incorrect. Blood pressure control remains essential for slowing progression and reducing CV events.
Incorrect. With eGFR 18, more frequent monitoring and active preparation are needed; waiting a year is inappropriate.
Incorrect. The brick endorses ACE/ARB and SGLT2 inhibitors as renoprotective; permanent discontinuation is not indicated.
